rename.from: Commands aren't able to fully gracefully exit by themselves
rename.to: [Console] Commands aren't able to fully gracefully exit by themselves

body:
We can workaround to this behaviour by setting `$app->setSignalsToDispatchEvent();` but that removes the dispatching of `ConsoleSignalEvent` or by implementing a custom `Application` class.

I don't think these are ideal solutions, though 😄
👍 To fix this. I think we can rely on the Application's `autoExit` flag

> +1 To fix this. I think we can rely on the Application's `autoExit` flag

I'm not sure if that's the way to go... we'd still want the application to exit with the code provided by the command's return.
@lyrixx perhaps you would have ideas here?

Stumbled across this too (https://github.com/symfony/symfony/discussions/48024)
How about not exit at all? Many of signals can be ignored, this is [intended behavior](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Termination-Signals.html#index-SIGTERM). Just call all of the handlers with `handleSignals` as last one and leave it to the developer to decide what to do next. For outside integrations there is SIGKILL that most of process managers sends after SIGTERM anyway, as it cannot be ignored and always result in process termination. (Yes, i know there is TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE kernel state in linux. But it is outside of the application scope)

@akuzia that's definitely the perfect idea. @lyrixx added that exit instruction, which got approved by @fabpot.

I'd gladly send a PR if that's the direction we want to go.

I added the exit instructions to mimic how php handle a sigterm.

With previous version of symfony, a sigterm does the same thing : it kills the application, isn't?

But maybe the list of signal we filter is not big enough?

Maybe I didn't understand your use case correctly.

> a sigterm does the same thing : it kills the application, isn't?

No. It signals application to exit. In which case developer can decide to gracefully exit or ignore this signal.
I've provided some code samples [here](https://github.com/symfony/symfony/discussions/48024#discussioncomment-3996082)

Ohh I think I understand. You are indeed listening to the signal but after your custom code it exists anyway but way too fast without calling other regular events. 

Did I understand correctly?

Dou you want to work on a PR? I can if you cannot, this is perfectly fine.

> > a sigterm does the same thing : it kills the application, isn't?
> 
> No. It signals application to exit. In which case developer can decide to gracefully exit or ignore this signal.

100% that!

The application should be the one in control here, not Symfony.

Just to make sure we're aligned, the goal of the PR is to remove the exit call, right?

Although I completely agree with that decision, it's a behavioural BC-break. Is Symfony alright with it?

as a user what would you except for each use cases?

1. **No** signal handler has been registered for SIGINT => the program exit as soon as possible

1. A signal handler has been been registered for SIGINT => Symfony execute your handler, and then do nothing, it means it'll resume your code "normally"

I agree this should be the default behavior. I added the exit because I wanted the mimic the default PHP behavior, but now I think I was wrong. Your [example](https://github.com/symfony/symfony/discussions/48024#discussioncomment-3996082) is really clear, and it should work as in the second case.

About 

> Although I completely agree with that decision, it's a behavioural BC-break. Is Symfony alright with it?

I don't know! cc @nicolas-grekas

Seems reasonable for any signal, not only SIGINT or SIGTERM (or any other one). I've used SIGHUP and SIGSTOP/SIGCONT several times with symfony.

> A signal handler has been been registered for SIGINT => Symfony execute your handler, and then do nothing, it means it'll resume your code "normally"

Yep, so `SignalableCommandInterface` becomes more of a convenience for registering async signal handlers and not the last signal handler.
